title: Why are Pentecostals growing so rapidly?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the rise of Pentecostalism, starting with the Azusa Street Revival led by William Seymour in Los Angeles in 1906 and the speaking-in-tongues practice that defines the movement. They trace its origins to Charles Parham in Topeka, the split along racial lines into the Church of God in Christ and the Assemblies of God, and the differences between Pentecostal, charismatic and evangelical beliefs, including baptism by the Holy Spirit. They cover the movement's rapid global growth, concentrated in the Global South, theories for why it spreads there (parallels with traditional religions and migration), and a listener mail about school janitors. Includes ad reads for the hosts' tour and an intro with a record plug.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour plug
segments.summary: Josh promotes upcoming tour dates in Vancouver and Portland and a friend's album, then the hosts introduce the topic of Pentecostalism and its status as a fast-growing Christian movement.

segments.title: Azusa Street Revival origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles led by William Seymour, where interracial congregations held services and people spoke in tongues, and the Los Angeles Times criticized it. They tie it to Pentecost in the Bible.

segments.title: Charles Parham and early Pentecostal founding
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Charles Parham in Topeka, Kansas, and church member Agnes Ozman speaking in tongues in 1901, and the role of speaking in tongues as the defining feature of Pentecostal belief in salvation.

segments.title: Racial split into Church of God in Christ and Assemblies of God
segments.summary: The hosts explain how a faction split from the Azusa Street mission, producing the largest US congregations: the predominantly African American Church of God in Christ and the predominantly white Assemblies of God.

segments.title: Global growth statistics of Pentecostalism
segments.summary: The hosts cite membership figures and growth: Pentecostals rose from 6 percent to 25 percent of global Christians by 2015, with about one in four Christians and one in twelve humans, concentrated in the Global South. Martin Mittelstadt is quoted on revival movements.

segments.title: Charismatic worship and personal experience of the Spirit
segments.summary: The hosts contrast structured liturgical worship with unstructured charismatic worship, where individuals have direct experiences of the Holy Spirit. Chuck and Josh share anecdotes about their church upbringing and attending a Pentecostal funeral.

segments.title: Water baptism vs. Spirit baptism and evangelical beliefs
segments.summary: The hosts explain the difference between water baptism and baptism by the Holy Spirit. They summarize David Bebington's four points defining evangelicals and explain that Pentecostals specifically require speaking in tongues as evidence of salvation.

segments.title: Speaking in tongues types and Azusa Street claims
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish xenoglossia, glossolalia, and spontaneous speech, note no documented cases of xenoglossia, and describe the Apostolic Faith Newspaper's claims about languages heard at Azusa Street and the missionary movement that followed.

segments.title: Why Pentecostalism grows in the Global South and migration
segments.summary: The hosts discuss statistics on conversions, the Redeemed Christian Church of God in Nigeria, Christians shifting to the Global South, and theories linking traditional spiritual worship to Pentecostalism. They also discuss migration among Christians and the double-edged nature of religious revivals, including the Second Great Awakening.

segments.title: Listener mail about high school janitors
segments.summary: Emily writes about her grandmother, a high school janitor in Gettysburg, South Dakota, and the hosts respond warmly.
